why_this_tool: nginx puts name resolution, connection reuse, TLS termination, HTTP versions and WebSocket upgrades into one small readable config file, so each network round trip and timeout in the lesson becomes a directive you can change and observe on a laptop.
alternatives: Envoy (dynamic API-driven configuration and first-class gRPC and observability, heavier to operate), HAProxy (very strong load balancing and connection-level statistics, less of a web server), Caddy (automatic certificates and a simpler config, fewer tuning knobs), Traefik (discovers routes from containers and orchestrators, less explicit control).

setup.do: Install a current stable nginx on your laptop with your package manager or as the official container image, and make sure curl, dig and openssl are available alongside it.
setup.done_when: Asking nginx for its version prints a stable release number that matches one on the download page.
setup.why: Every later step changes nginx configuration and observes the effect from a client, so you need a known nginx version and the three client tools.

setup.do: Open the main configuration file, find the main, events and http contexts, set the error log to a file you can tail and start nginx.
setup.done_when: nginx is running, its pid file exists and a deliberately broken directive shows up as an error in the log you configured.
setup.why: Knowing where the top-level directives live and where errors are written is what makes every later experiment quick to debug.

setup.do: Start a tiny local backend on a high port, for example a small echo server that also accepts WebSocket connections, to act as the upstream nginx will proxy to.
setup.done_when: A direct curl request to the backend port returns its response without nginx involved.
setup.why: The proxying, timeout and WebSocket steps need something behind nginx, and the proxy module page explains what nginx expects from a proxied server.

steps.do: Write a first server block that listens on a local port and returns a fixed response from one location, then request it with curl in verbose mode.
steps.done_when: curl verbose output shows the connection being opened and a 200 response carrying your fixed body.
steps.why: This is the first run: you see the TCP connect, the request line, the response status and headers that every later step will change.

steps.do: Create two virtual servers on the same port with different server names, map both names to loopback in your hosts file, and query each name with dig and curl.
steps.done_when: Each name returns a different body from the same address and port, and an unknown name lands on the default server.
steps.why: DNS only gets the client to an address; the Host header then picks the server block, and seeing both halves separately is the core object model of nginx.

steps.do: Configure the resolver directive with a short validity time and proxy to an upstream named through a variable so nginx resolves the name at request time rather than at startup.
steps.done_when: Changing what the upstream name resolves to takes effect after the validity time without reloading nginx, and a failing resolver produces a visible error in the log.
steps.why: DNS is the first hop for the proxy too: a name resolved once at startup goes stale, and the resolver settings decide when that lookup round trip and its timeout happen.

steps.do: Configure a location that proxies to your local backend and passes the original Host and client address in request headers.
steps.done_when: The backend echo shows the Host and client address headers you set, and the response arrives through the nginx port.
steps.why: A reverse proxy means two separate connections, client to nginx and nginx to backend, and a designer must know what information crosses that boundary.

steps.do: Set short proxy connect, send and read timeouts, then reproduce each one by pointing at a closed port and at a backend that sleeps before answering.
steps.done_when: You get a 502 for the refused connection and a 504 for the slow backend, each with a matching error log line.
steps.why: Timeouts are where hidden state lives in a design; triggering each one tells you which phase failed and what status the client sees.

steps.do: Configure the client keepalive timeout and the keepalive request limit, then send several requests in one curl invocation and compare with keepalive disabled.
steps.done_when: curl verbose output reports reusing the existing connection with keepalive on and opening a new connection per request with it off.
steps.why: Connection reuse removes the TCP handshake from every request after the first, and the limits decide how long that idle state is held on the server.

steps.do: Create a self-signed certificate for your local name and configure an HTTPS server on a second port with that certificate and key.
steps.done_when: curl with the certificate trusted completes a TLS handshake and returns your response, and it fails with a name mismatch when you use the wrong host name.
steps.why: Terminating TLS at the proxy adds handshake round trips and a certificate that must match the name, which is the cost you reason about in a design.

steps.do: Configure the allowed TLS protocol versions and a shared session cache with a session timeout, then reconnect with the openssl client to compare a full handshake with a resumed one.
steps.done_when: The openssl client reports a reused session on reconnect with the cache enabled and a new session each time with it disabled.
steps.why: Session resumption is the TLS form of reuse: it cuts the handshake cost for returning clients and is shared state across worker processes.

steps.do: Enable HTTP/2 on the HTTPS server and compare the same set of requests made with curl forced to HTTP/1.1 and to HTTP/2.
steps.done_when: curl reports HTTP/2 as the negotiated protocol and several requests travel on a single connection, while the forced HTTP/1.1 run shows the older version in the status line.
steps.why: The protocol version changes how requests share a connection: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams on one connection where HTTP/1.1 needs one request at a time per connection.

steps.do: Configure a location that proxies WebSocket traffic by passing the Upgrade and Connection headers to the backend over HTTP/1.1, then connect with a WebSocket client.
steps.done_when: The client receives a 101 Switching Protocols response and messages echo in both directions through nginx.
steps.why: The upgrade is a hop-by-hop handshake that a proxy drops unless told to forward it, which is the most common reason WebSockets fail behind a proxy.

steps.do: Reproduce the idle close of a silent WebSocket connection at the default proxy read timeout, then fix it by raising the timeout or by having the backend send periodic pings.
steps.done_when: A silent connection is closed after about a minute before the change and stays open well past that after it.
steps.why: Long-lived connections are held open by timers on every hop, so a design must choose between longer timeouts and heartbeats.

steps.do: Check the security advisories for your nginx version, pin a non-vulnerable release in your container image tag or package version, and keep the whole configuration in one versioned file.
steps.done_when: A fresh container or install built from the pinned version and your config file passes all earlier checks, and no listed advisory applies to that version.
steps.why: A pinned version and a single config file make the setup reproducible on another machine and tell you when an upgrade is required.

steps.do: Configure a production-like process model with automatic worker processes, an explicit worker connection limit and open file limit, then reload the configuration while a WebSocket connection is open.
steps.done_when: Several worker processes are running, the reload applies new settings without dropping the open WebSocket, and the old worker exits once that connection closes.
steps.why: Worker and connection limits cap how many concurrent and long-lived connections one machine holds, and a graceful reload shows how old workers drain them.
